body.text: Some vendors already contemplate this scenario. For example, Microsoft documents a warehouse-only mode that can run alongside another vendor's ERP, which shows the warehouse and the ERP can be decided separately.
When does the ERP's inventory module stop being enough?

The signals tend to be operational, but their effect reaches leadership: frequent differences between system and physical inventory, full counts that stop operations, orders that ship incomplete or late even though the system showed stock, picking times that grow with every new customer, and operators who depend on one person who knows where everything is. If two or three of these keep recurring, the cost is already in your margin even if it has no line of its own on the income statement.
What should leadership ask before buying a WMS?

Before requesting quotes, answer four questions. First, what is the problem in business terms: lost sales from stockouts, capital tied up in inventory, labor cost per order or missed deliveries. Second, what is the five-year total cost, which includes licenses or subscription, implementation, ERP integration, scanning devices and maintenance; the same logic as what it costs to implement an enterprise system applies here. Third, who sustains the system after go-live. And fourth, what happens to operations on cutover day: a WMS is largely configured with rules, and those rules are tested before they reach the floor.

body.text: How do you choose a WMS?

Start by describing your real operation —type of product, number of warehouses, order lines per day, seasonal peaks, traceability requirements— not a vendor's catalog. With that written down, ask each vendor for a demo using your own flows and talk to customers of similar size and sector. Weigh especially the integration with your current ERP, the ecosystem of implementers in your country and how easily your team can adjust the rules without depending on the vendor. A well-chosen but poorly adopted WMS doesn't fix inventory.

body.text: SAP Business One is SAP's ERP for mid-sized companies. Asking what it costs is reasonable, but the honest answer starts elsewhere: there is no single figure, and whoever gives you one without knowing your operation is guessing.
A disclosure before we continue: Cyrrus doesn't resell licenses or take commissions from any vendor. That's why we can explain the cost without preferences.
Does SAP publish the price of Business One?

No. As of October 2026, SAP's site shows no list price for Business One: it is bought through implementation partners, who quote based on scope, region and deployment model (cloud or your own infrastructure). Per-user figures circulating on third-party blogs are estimates from partners or resellers, differ from each other and age quickly; use them as an order of magnitude to start the conversation, never as a budget.
What drives the license cost?

A Business One license is per named user, and each person has a type. According to SAP's license guide, the types are Professional (broad access to functionality), Limited (Financials, Logistics and CRM, for operational staff with narrower access) and Starter Package, which allows a maximum of five users, can't be combined with other types and excludes advanced functions. Classifying each person correctly before quoting is one of the decisions that moves the price the most. The Android mobile app carries no additional fee for these user types. The license guide cited is for version 10.0, so confirm the current terms for your version with the partner.

Calculate the five-year cost: licenses or subscription plus support multiplied by five, plus implementation, integrations, infrastructure and internal team time. Ask at least three partners for the same proposal with the same scope, and demand the breakdown by block: compare hours and assumptions, not just the total. A cheap proposal with a narrow scope tends to end in change orders. Our article on what it costs to implement an ERP details the hidden costs that most often derail budgets.

body.text: A CMMS (computerized maintenance management system) is the software that schedules, assigns and records maintenance work: work orders, preventive maintenance, spare parts and each machine's history. An EAM (enterprise asset management) does that and also follows the asset throughout its life, from purchase to retirement.
A disclosure before we continue: Cyrrus doesn't resell licenses or take commissions from any vendor. That's why we can compare without preferences.
What is the difference between a CMMS and an EAM?

A CMMS focuses on the maintenance stage and is used mostly by maintenance and production teams, with the goal of avoiding unexpected downtime. An EAM spans the whole lifecycle and also involves finance, operations and management, because it includes planning for new assets, risk analysis and performance analysis. The products overlap and many vendors use the two terms interchangeably, so compare real functions, not labels.

body.text: When is a CMMS enough and when is an EAM justified?

A full CMMS is usually enough when the problem is execution: paper work orders, uncontrolled spare parts, reactive maintenance. An EAM is justified when leadership's question is about the portfolio: when to replace an asset, how much to invest in each plant, what risk to accept. As CMMS products add EAM-type functions the gap narrows, which is why a cost-benefit analysis makes sense before paying for the extra features.
What should leadership measure to justify the investment?

Before asking for demos, measure what you can't see today: what an hour of unplanned downtime costs on your critical lines, what share of work is preventive versus corrective, how much is spent on emergency spare parts and how many critical machines lack a reliable history. With that data the business case writes itself, and it also lets you measure the result a year later.
How does it connect to the ERP?

Maintenance consumes spare parts, generates purchases and charges costs to accounting. A poor integration forces double entry or manual reconciliation. Before choosing, define which system is the source of truth for the equipment master, the spare-parts inventory and costs, and who maintains the integration. If you haven't chosen the ERP yet, decide both together.
How do you choose maintenance software?

Start from your real operation: equipment criticality, number of plants, technical staff and how work is logged today. Ask for a demo with your own assets and test field use with two or three technicians on the device they will actually use. If you want to certify your asset management, the ISO 55000 family sets the framework: ISO 55001 establishes the requirements of an asset management system and applies to any type and size of organization.

body.text: SAP ECC (part of SAP Business Suite 7, with SAP ERP 6.0 at its core) is the ERP many mid-sized and large Latin American companies run on. SAP S/4HANA is its successor. The debate is no longer whether to migrate, but when, how and at what cost.

What dates has SAP set for ECC?
The official dates haven't changed since SAP's 2020 announcement, and SAP restated them in October 2026.

body.text: What happens if I don't migrate in time?

The system doesn't switch off on January 1, 2028: it keeps running. What changes is the vendor's backing and the cost of staying where you are. There is also a critical date for those on third-party databases: according to SAP, converting a Business Suite 7 system with a third-party database to S/4HANA or SAP Cloud ERP is only possible until the end of 2030; after that only a new implementation remains. Waiting has an opportunity cost, because it narrows your options just when teams and vendors are most stretched.

body.text: What should leadership decide before requesting quotes?

First, the route and the business goal: what you want to simplify or enable, not just meet a date. Second, the scope of customizations: each one you keep is paid for in the migration and in every future update. Third, sponsorship and who manages the project on the company side. Fourth, the total budget, which must include internal team time, training and change management on top of licenses and services; our article on what it costs to implement an ERP details those blocks. And fifth, a calendar with slack against 2027 and 2030. Ignoring the human side is the costliest mistake: our organizational change management guide explains how to avoid it.

body.text: HR software is the set of systems where a company keeps its employees' data and runs the processes that depend on it: hiring, payroll, absences, performance and development. The label changes by vendor, and that confusion is the first cause of comparisons that aren't comparable.
A disclosure before we continue: Cyrrus doesn't resell licenses or take commissions from any vendor. That's why we can compare without preferences.
What is the difference between payroll, HRIS and HCM?

Payroll software calculates and pays. An HRIS (human resources information system) manages the employee record: data, contracts, benefits, history. An HCM (human capital management) includes that and adds the rest of the lifecycle: recruiting, shift scheduling, absences, performance reviews, training and analytics. Vendors don't draw these lines the same way; some include payroll inside the HRIS and others treat it as a component of the HCM.

body.text: What changes when the company passes 100 employees?

What's at stake changes. Payroll errors stop being rework and become legal and reputational exposure. Turnover and absenteeism start to weigh on the margin. And leadership needs reliable personnel-cost figures, which today usually come from spreadsheets. If the company operates in several countries, each brings its own labor and payroll legislation, and the system must support it or rely on a local partner; that often decides which alternatives are viable before you compare features.
How does it integrate with finance and the ERP?

Payroll is one of the company's largest expenses and must reach accounting without rework. Before choosing, define which system is the source of truth for the employee master, the organizational structures and cost centers, and who maintains the integration. If you haven't chosen the ERP yet, decide both together; doing it separately multiplies the interfaces.
What should leadership decide before quoting?

First, the problem in business terms: compliance risk, process cost, turnover or lack of data to decide. Second, the geographic and legal scope. Third, who owns the system: HR, finance or IT. Fourth, personal data protection, which in HR includes sensitive information and demands role-based access controls. And fifth, the multi-year total cost, using the same logic as what it costs to implement an enterprise system, plus your team's time.

body.text: How do you choose HR software?

Start from your real processes and the countries where you operate. Ask each vendor for a demo with your own case, including a real test payroll, and talk to customers of similar size and regions. Test the experience of managers and employees, because adoption depends on it. And verify who is responsible for legal changes in each country. A well-chosen but poorly adopted system still forces people back into spreadsheets.

body.text: An MES (manufacturing execution system) is software designed for the factory. It coordinates, records and monitors production from raw materials to finished goods, and sits between the ERP and the plant control systems.
A disclosure before we continue: Cyrrus doesn't resell licenses or take commissions from any vendor. That's why we can compare without preferences.
What does an MES do?

It receives work orders from the ERP and schedules them by priorities and available resources; dispatches the work to lines and people; allocates and tracks labor, materials and machines; keeps a two-way data exchange with the floor to correct in real time; controls documents, quality and traceability by lot, serial or order number; and collects production data to measure performance. When finished, it returns the results to the ERP.
What is the difference between an MES and an ERP?

The ERP manages the business as a whole: long-term planning, purchasing, costing and customer orders. The MES manages execution on the plant floor. The ISA-95 standard (IEC 62264) describes how they communicate: it places the ERP at level 4 (business planning) and the MES at level 3 (manufacturing operations management), and focuses on the interface between the two.
Where each system lives in a plant
rows: What should we produce and at what cost?
What is happening in the plant right now and how is it executed?
How does the physical process run?

body.text: When does a plant need an MES?

Not every plant does. The clearest signals are these: lot or serial traceability is a customer or regulatory requirement; quality is critical and defects are found late; the ERP's plan and what happens on the floor diverge and nobody sees it until month-end; downtime and cycle times are logged by hand; or several plants run on different rules. If none apply, a good production setup in the ERP may be enough.
What should leadership ask before investing?

Four things. First, which decision you can't make today for lack of plant data, and what not making it costs. Second, how it will integrate with the ERP, who maintains the interface and what happens when either changes. Third, the multi-year total cost, using the logic of what it costs to implement an enterprise system, including devices, plant networks and supervisors' time. And fourth, how go-live will happen without stopping production.

body.text: How do you choose an MES?

Start from your real process: type of production, number of plants, quality and traceability requirements, and the plant team available. Ask for demos with your own flows, visit similar customers' plants and weigh integration with your current ERP. Test the screen with real operators: if it gets in their way they won't use it, and an MES that isn't logged on time doesn't do its job.
